questions.enonce_markdown: Draw the truth table for each of the propositions $p \Rightarrow q$ and $\sim p \lor q$ and show that they are identical. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Recall that $p \Rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false, and that $\sim p$ means "not $p$". The proposition $\sim p \lor q$ is read $(\sim p) \lor q$, true when at least one of $\sim p$, $q$ is true.

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \Rightarrow q$ | $\sim p$ | $\sim p \lor q$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| T | T | T | F | T |
| T | F | F | F | F |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | T | T | T |

Row by row:

- $p = T, q = T$: $p \Rightarrow q$ is T; $\sim p = F$, so $F \lor T = T$.
- $p = T, q = F$: $p \Rightarrow q$ is F; $\sim p = F$, so $F \lor F = F$.
- $p = F, q = T$: $p \Rightarrow q$ is T; $\sim p = T$, so $T \lor T = T$.
- $p = F, q = F$: $p \Rightarrow q$ is T; $\sim p = T$, so $T \lor F = T$.

The columns for $p \Rightarrow q$ and $\sim p \lor q$ are the same in all four rows (T, F, T, T), so the two propositions are logically equivalent (identical): $p \Rightarrow q \equiv\ \sim p \lor q$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\sin^{-1}(x) = \alpha$ and $\cos^{-1}(x) = \beta$, show that $\sin(\alpha + \beta) = 1$. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The inverse functions are defined for $-1 \le x \le 1$, with principal values $\alpha = \sin^{-1}x \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and $\beta = \cos^{-1}x \in [0, \pi]$.

From the definitions: $\sin\alpha = x$ and $\cos\beta = x$.

**Find the other two ratios.**

- On $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\cos\alpha \ge 0$, so $\cos\alpha = +\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\alpha} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$.
- On $[0, \pi]$, $\sin\beta \ge 0$, so $\sin\beta = +\sqrt{1 - \cos^2\beta} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$.

**Compound angle formula.**

$$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta = x\cdot x + \sqrt{1 - x^2}\cdot\sqrt{1 - x^2} = x^2 + (1 - x^2) = 1. \qquad \blacksquare$$

(Remark: this shows $\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, i.e. $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$; e.g. $x = \dfrac12$: $\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.)
